title: Super Micro contractor pleads guilty in scheme to divert AI servers with Nvidia chips to China
author: Daniel Nenni
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun, a contractor associated with Super Micro Computer, pleaded guilty in Manhattan federal court on October 8 to four counts involving the illegal export of AI servers to China. Reuters reported that the counts included conspiracies to violate export controls, smuggle goods, defraud the United States and obstruct justice. His lawyer declined to comment.

The case concerns an alleged network that used a Southeast Asian company to acquire servers containing restricted American AI technology. Prosecutors charged Sun alongside Super Micro co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw and Ruei-Tsang “Steven” Chang, who worked in the manufacturer’s Taiwan office.

According to the Justice Department, the intermediary bought approximately $2.5 billion in servers during 2024 and 2025. Prosecutors alleged that at least $510 million worth reached China during a period spanning late April and mid-May 2025.

The alleged operation relied on false records identifying the intermediary as the servers’ final user. Shipments passed through Taiwan and Southeast Asia, where equipment was repackaged in unmarked boxes before being sent to China.

Investigators also described elaborate efforts to mislead compliance teams and government inspectors. Nonworking replica servers were displayed at warehouses after genuine equipment had already been diverted. Sun allegedly helped prepare those replicas, transferring labels and serial-number stickers to make them appear authentic. Participants coordinated orders, destinations and concealment through encrypted messaging applications.

American export rules require licenses for transferring certain advanced AI chips and servers to China because of national security concerns. Authorities argue that access to this computing power can strengthen military capabilities.

Super Micro said it was not a defendant and that the case had not affected business operations. It previously terminated Sun and severed ties with the other defendants.

The case illustrates why checking shipment destinations and verifying actual equipment matter when enforcing restrictions across complex international technology supply chains.
